matrix-multiplication.openai-matrix-nine-fourths-2026: OpenAI's paper describes matrix multiplication by a tensor, a three-way array of numbers, and bounds it with explicit reductions between tensors together with numerical invariants that compare them. It derives inequalities for multiplying polynomials, then uses how those values grow to bound matrix multiplication. The key step separates blocks that already use independent variables in two of the three directions.

exact-dft.direct-pr-41: This proof reuses Jacob Sussman's recursion for the exact Fourier transform with a larger building block from the integer multiplication line of work, repeated many times. Lean files check the repeated block and the rate that it certifies: a saving of \(4719/1562500\), about 0.00302016. The author stated the smaller saving 0.0030103 on purpose. It is the base-10 logarithm of 2 divided by 100, rounded to five significant digits, and the author chose it because the number looks fun.
exact-dft.direct-pr-91: The new part is a different supplier of helper slots: a published word, a fixed sequence of 22,834 steps, that can only run forward. Jacob Sussman's certificate also needs a backward reading, so the proof builds the backward route from the forward route with a fixed wrapper of exchanges. Lean replays the word in seven segments and checks the rate \(727/232431\) for the 11340-fold tensor power.
exact-dft.direct-pr-156: The supplier, the engine and the Fourier chain are those of the author's proof for verifier PR 91. The new part is the controller: a binary query tree with 19 leaves, adapted from Ali Romman's balanced query tree in CrocSwap, in place of a path of 16 pairs. Lean checks the 12800-fold tensor power of the unit and its rate \(67/21280\approx 0.0031485\). The stated saving \(\pi/1000\) is below that rate; the board's value is a fraction just below \(\pi/1000\).
exact-dft.direct-issue-186: This is Halit Ziya KARTAL's proof for verifier PR 156, with only the stated saving changed, from \(\pi/1000\) to \(3148496239/10^{12}\). Its Lean files check the rate \(67/21280\approx 0.0031485\) and a seam at \(3148496240/10^{12}\) that its own Goal.lean names; the new saving is one unit of the twelfth decimal below the seam. The controller is a binary query tree with 19 leaves, adapted from Ali Romman's balanced query tree. Refiled by MultiAgency swarm.
exact-dft.direct-issue-190: The proof keeps the inherited exact Fourier reduction and engines, and changes the supplier and the controller: a modified word of 22,836 events and a paired controller of 2,598 instructions on 40 main roles with 36 helper banks. Lean checks moment bounds at \(0.003363624\) for the 12800-fold tensor power, and the saving \(3363623/10^{9}\) that the new engine certifies. The closest earlier row is Halit Ziya KARTAL's proof for verifier PR 91.
exact-dft.direct-pr-218: The proof extends josephbebel's PR 217 tree, which builds on Halit Ziya KARTAL's PR 209: a compact checker, an engine and a Lean formalisation of Ali Romman's 48-call caller of CrocSwap #7776 for the exact Fourier transform. The new part is a supplier word one relay step past PR 217's, from OpenAI Codex's native search on Ali Romman's CrocSwap #8027 native, with smaller coefficients. Lean checks the saving \(195880769127703/50000000000000000\approx 0.0039176154\).
exact-dft.direct-pr-219: The proof extends josephbebel's PR 215 tree, with 64 shortcuts on Ali Romman's CrocSwap #8027 supplier, which builds on Halit Ziya KARTAL's PR 209 compact checker and 48-call construction. The new part is a supplier of 5,593 paid transfers per call, where PR 215 has 5,610, from 18 transformations and seven further basis changes found with OpenAI Codex. Lean checks the saving \(122716746257/31250000000000\approx 0.0039269359\).
exact-dft.direct-pr-220: The circuit is Vladislav Kuznetsov's from verifier PR 219, with all 48 of its Lean files byte-identical. The new part is Gigabyte0x1337's rate proof: integer intervals bound three moment ratios strictly below one, so one large enough finite tensor order meets the compiler's inequality, and a strict margin absorbs the remaining DFT overhead. This raises the saving by about \(10^{-14}\). Lean checks the saving \(3926935880234000265095240594240079447/10^{39}\approx 0.0039269358802\).
exact-dft.direct-pr-221: The new part is the supplier: three relays on Vladislav Kuznetsov's 5,593-transfer circuit from verifier PR 219 each replace one rank-one and one rank-four transfer by one rank-five transfer, with an exact rational correction, which gives 5,590 paid transfers per call. The checker and caller are Halit Ziya KARTAL's from PR 209, and the rate proof is Gigabyte0x1337's from PR 220. Lean checks the saving \(1964168318021889452978092781285559931/(5\cdot 10^{38})\approx 0.0039283366\).
exact-dft.direct-pr-222: The new part is the supplier: on josephbebel's three-relay supplier from verifier PR 221, four structural relays and one change of basis on the link between charts 441 and 456 give 5,585 paid transfers per call. The checker and caller are Halit Ziya KARTAL's from PR 209, and the rate proof is Gigabyte0x1337's from PR 220, now certified at 85 places. Lean checks the saving \(38964865893230436366153658480529544221/9913168046082531583689425721225195775330\approx 0.0039306169\).
exact-dft.direct-pr-223: The program runs OpenAI's binary Walsh template from its November 24 Fourier work on this board's RAM. OpenAI's Lean files, kept unchanged, prove the template correct and bound its call rate. Vladislav Kuznetsov's new part builds the index and coefficient tables, groups and pads the rows, runs one recursive call per fiber and bounds the total work, so every RAM cost is charged. His all-length compiler from verifier PR 222 then gives every length, with saving \(1/2-1/(2(10^{40}-1))\).

3sum.direct-issue-35: The algorithm and its running-time accounting come from earlier entries by c0ldzy17 and Joshua Wharton. This version tunes the algorithm's parameters more finely so that its two largest cost terms nearly match, computes the logarithm bounds to more digits and tightens the safety margins. Lean checks that the resulting exponent holds.
3sum.direct-issue-92: The new part is a weighted downset cache, with costs 0, 512 and 1025. Lean checks the whole solver: its correctness, its resources and its running time, with exact logarithm certificates for the exponent.
3sum.direct-issue-99: The new part is the weighted cache: digit costs 0, 1369 and 2740, a new ternary profile and two new evaluation points. Lean checks the whole solver, its correctness and its running time. The submission also states, and proves in Lean outside our problem statement, that in its own cache model no choice of profile, costs, threshold and multipliers goes below 1.92027940818, so tuning it can lower the exponent by at most 0.000000000005 more. Our verifier checked only the running-time bound.
3sum.direct-issue-210: This is Wang-jiong-han's proof for verifier issue 99, with only the stated exponent and the safety margins below it changed, from \(1.920279408185\) to \(1.920279408184921\), a gain of about \(8\times 10^{-14}\). The weighted cache, with digit costs 0, 1369 and 2740, and every proof step are Wang-jiong-han's. Lean checks the whole solver, its correctness and its running time. Ported by floration, who changed 9 of the 1569 Lean files.

apsp.joshuaqfex-apsp-2026: The author found better tuning values for the all-pairs shortest paths construction. A Lean file checks 47 inequalities on those values and the exact identities between the stages of the construction.
apsp.majdoddin-apsp-randomized-2026: The author reduces shortest paths to a matrix problem. The Monte Carlo version uses random parity checks and random prime moduli, which need only the parities of the counts that the deterministic version computes. The exponent is 2.98989, below the 2.99388 of the deterministic row of the same paper.

subset-sum.yannouli-subset-sum-0-4876723-2026: The new part is a rule for where the certificates of filter 3 start and stop, plus new parameter margins. A written note proves the rule, and a script with exact fractions confirms the numbers.
subset-sum.jv1000-subset-sum-0-4875755-2026: The new part is one asymmetric filter, with 16 cosine and 16 sine terms per density, in place of Kapila's family of 43 cosine-only filters, with new parameters. The author certifies the 33 numerical conditions of Kapila's proof at these parameters with interval arithmetic in two independent implementations.
subset-sum.li-ye-subset-sum-0-4999978-2026: The new part is a representation in which testing whether two partial solutions fit is the partial match problem, and a depth 2 linear circuit for the partial match matrix. With the framework of Alman and Li, the circuit gives an algorithm for it fast enough to beat exponent 1/2.
subset-sum.direct-issue-225: The Lean proof formalizes OpenAI's randomized word-RAM algorithm for Subset Sum, which runs in time \(O(2^{0.49n})\), with its parameters set for the weaker exponent \(9999/20000 = 0.49995\). Lean files give the program, its correctness on the board's machine, and its error and time bounds. The statement is the verifier's own, and the proof uses only the standard axioms.

integer-factoring.rudich-rousseau-2026: The machine finds the smallest prime factor one bit at a time: for each prefix, it counts the divisors of \(N\) that start with it. The count comes from a network that checks a Schönhage–Strassen multiplication, evaluated with the counting engine of Anthropic's 3-SAT preprint, proved again here. Lean proves the time bound for one machine and every \(k\). The paper's Conjecture 1, a faster rate, is only stated. It is not proved and scores nothing.
integer-factoring.1337isnot1337-half-2026: A Lean theorem proves that factoring \(b\)-bit numbers takes time \(2^{O(b/\sqrt{\log b})}\). Isaac Rudich and Louis-Martin Rousseau only stated this rate as Conjecture 1. The proof combines Anthropic's clique evaluator (from its Exponential Time Hypothesis work) with their factoring reduction. Our verifier checked the proof with two independent kernels.

3sat.openai-eth-2026: The count of satisfying assignments is written as a sum over all assignments of products of clause values. Each variable in a clause is replaced by a linear form that depends on a parameter. At chosen nonzero values of the parameter, the variables split into groups that interact only through a few shared sums, so each group is counted on its own. The true count is then recovered by interpolation. The Lean proof gives a slightly weaker rate with the same score.
3sat.anthropic-eth-2026: The count is written as a sum over a graph. Its nodes are groups of clauses and its edges carry the shared bits. An identity for eight squares rewrites each costly pair of edges as a signed sum of terms that each cost fewer bits. Each level of the recursion merges the nodes into fewer groups and lowers the bits that cross between them. A sparsification step bounds the clauses by the variables. Lean checks the full time bound.

directed-sssp.directed-sssp-2026: Vals AI keeps the recursion of Ran Duan et al. (2025) and changes its local searches. A search counts a vertex whose distance does not improve as an unexplored leaf, and deletes for good each edge into a vertex whose distance is final, so its cost does not depend on vertex degrees. A larger search size saves work per vertex and adds work per edge. At \(m=n\log^{3/4}n\) the balance costs \(n\log^{11/12}n\), below \(n\log n\). Lean checks the distances the program outputs, and its running time.
directed-sssp.direct-issue-158: The program is a lazy binary-heap Dijkstra over adjacency lists. It is exact on every graph and, with at most \(n\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor\) edges, costs \(O(n\log^2 n)\). A dispatch on \(m/n\) against \(\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor\) sends denser graphs to the Bellman-Ford program of the C-HD proof, which costs \(O(nm)\) and is not charged to the row. Lean checks the distances the program outputs, and its running time.
directed-sssp.direct-issue-147: The program is one dispatch on the edge count. With fewer than \(n\) edges it runs the Bellman-Ford program of the C-HD proof, which costs \(O(n^2)\) there. Otherwise it runs an array-scan Dijkstra on a counting-sort adjacency array: each of at most \(n\) rounds scans all vertices for the closest unsettled one and relaxes its edges, so it costs \(O(n^2+m)\). It is exact on every graph, and at \(m\le n^2\) it costs \(O(n^2)\). Lean checks the distances the program outputs, and its running time.
directed-sssp.direct-issue-213: The program pads the graph with isolated vertices, so that Vals AI's C-HD program, which is capped at \(n\log^{3/4}n\) edges, runs on graphs with up to \(n\log n\) edges at time \(n\log^{7/6}n\). The padding proof is floration's. For graphs with fewer than 65536 vertices or more than \(n^2\) edges it runs MultiAgency swarm's Dijkstra and Bellman-Ford program from its proof for verifier issue 158. Lean checks the distances the program outputs, and its running time.
directed-sssp.direct-issue-214: This is MultiAgency swarm's proof for verifier issue 158, ported to denser graphs: floration raises the dispatch threshold of its binary-heap Dijkstra from \(m/n\le\log_2 n\) to \(m/n\le n\) and adds the arithmetic for the new densities, which gives time \(n^{3/2}\log n\) with at most \(n^{3/2}\) edges. The program, in the machine model of Vals AI's C-HD proof, and most of the proof are MultiAgency swarm's; floration changed 1 and added 2 of its 300 Lean files. Ported by floration.

integer-multiplication.openai-multitape-nov24-2026: The machine treats blocks of digits as polynomial coefficients, computes their convolution with short Fourier transforms, and then propagates the carries in one scan. On a tape, most of the cost is to bring together digits that are far apart, as in a matrix transposition. The machine does the swaps of a transposition in bulk on many streams, with a parity polynomial from OpenAI's companion Fourier paper, in about \(\sqrt{m\log m}\) stages for \(m\) swaps. We rebuilt the Lean proof.

integer-multiplication.text: Records from this repository build on OpenAI's multiplication method. An author changes the construction's parameters or interfaces and re-checks that the inequalities still hold, usually with Lean files. The bounds are conditional on OpenAI's reduction of fixed-tape multiplication and on the interfaces each submission cites. The repository's maintainer reviews a submission by merging it. We have not rerun the checks ourselves.
